planting.note: Set out container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; sapphireberry fruits most heavily where a second unrelated seedling or cultivar is planted nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Sapphireberry is an East Asian relative of the native southern sweetleaf, grown as a large shade-tolerant shrub or small tree for its clusters of fragrant creamy-white spring flowers and, more famously, its abundant fall crop of small, intensely metallic-blue drupes. The vivid berries persist on bare branches well into winter since birds are often slow to find them, making this an excellent four-season specimen at the edge of a woodland garden or shrub border. It flowers and fruits best with several hours of direct sun but tolerates the dappled light of a partial-shade understory site reasonably well. Because old wood carries the heaviest bloom, limit pruning to shaping cuts made right after flowering rather than removing large older limbs.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this close relative of the hardier bee-bee tree needs a sheltered warm-temperate site and benefits from winter mulch in its coldest tolerated zones.

directions: Closely related to the better-known Korean bee-bee tree, this small-to-medium East Asian tree bears the same flat-topped clusters of tiny greenish-white flowers in late summer, opening at a time when few other trees are blooming and drawing heavy, audible honeybee traffic from a considerable distance. The compound leaves have a pungent, citrus-like scent when crushed, and the small reddish fruit capsules split to reveal shiny black seeds valued in traditional Chinese herbal preparations. Give it a sunny site with good air movement and room to develop its broad, rounded crown, since crowding promotes the twiggy dieback this species is prone to in humid climates. It makes an unusual specimen tree for a pollinator garden where late-season nectar flow is a priority.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; like its American cousin this species resents root disturbance, so choose a permanent site and avoid later transplanting.

directions: Chinese sassafras is the East Asian counterpart to the familiar native sassafras, sharing the same aromatic bark and foliage but growing into a noticeably larger forest tree with broader, less consistently lobed leaves. Small yellow-green flower clusters open before the leaves in early spring, followed later by dark, berry-like fruits on red stalks that are quickly taken by birds. It is still uncommon outside botanical collections and large arboreta, where it is grown chiefly as a handsome shade tree with excellent fall color ranging through yellow, orange, and scarlet on the same plant. Because it is dioecious, a female tree needs a nearby male to set the ornamental fruit display.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this Korean island endemic wants the warm, humid, frost-light conditions of the Gulf Coast's milder zones to establish well.

directions: Native to Jeju Island and the warm southern coast of Korea, this glossy-leaved evergreen tree is best known historically for its golden sap, once harvested to lacquer royal furniture and artifacts in a technique far rarer and more labor-intensive than ordinary Asian lacquer work. Its leathery, variably lobed leaves and small umbels of greenish flowers followed by dark purple-black fruit give it a refined, almost tropical look in a shaded garden setting. Because it comes from a mild coastal climate, it performs best in the warmest, most sheltered partial-shade sites available and appreciates protection from drying winter wind at the northern edge of its range. It is increasingly grown in warm-temperate collections as an understory specimen prized for its year-round foliage.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; young trees are notably shade-tolerant and establish well as an understory planting before eventually growing into the canopy.

directions: Shii is a broadleaf evergreen member of the beech family long grown throughout Japan both as a street and shade tree and as an orchard nut tree, producing small acorn-like nuts in a spiny, lobed cupule that can be roasted and eaten much like a small chestnut. Its glossy, leathery leaves have a distinctive bronze sheen when young, maturing to dark green, and the tree's dense, rounded crown makes it a durable choice for warm coastal gardens that can handle salt-laden wind. Nut set improves where more than one seedling is planted nearby, and trees need several years of establishment before bearing a meaningful crop. Once mature, the thick canopy also makes shii a useful large-scale screening or windbreak tree in frost-light landscapes.
